SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
tremely concentrated loads lead to a more significant decrease in functional indices and to a 
disruption in adaptation (graph fj).
When using concentrated loads orientated to achieving the LDTE, the methods used should 
not be extremely intense. Concentration, in one of the single purpose loads, is already in­
tensification of the training effect and to increase it with highly intense means of training 
does not follow.
Realization of LDTE of concentrated loads is served by moderate increases in work volume 
and gradually increasing intensity (B).
. 
The duration of the appearance of LDTE is determined by the volume and duration of the 
concentrated loads used. In principle, the steady appearance of LDTE (t2 ) is equal to the du­
ration of the stage (ti). In real conditions of training high level athletes, the tendency has 
been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks. It follows, however, to keep in mind 
that the appearance of LDTE has an independent character and to a significant degree, de­
pends upon the ability of the athlete to withstand volume loads and the ability of his body 
for recovery. The same volume loads in two athletes having the same qualifications can 
have a different effect.
>. 
In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body rela­
tively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work 
volume. The latter is expressed by a slowdown in increases and even a decrease in the func­
tional abilities. For example. Figure 8 shows that in triple jumpers, after the concentrated 
specialized strength preparation loads in March-April, the LDTE acquired showed an in­
crease in speed-strength and increased sports results in May-June.

Development of the adaptation process is tied in with a definite heterochronicity in the formation 
of accommodative body restructuring. Heterochronicity appears first in the failure to coincide 
moments of time with the corresponding beginnings of the intense improvement of one or an­
other functional system. Second, it appears in the specific consecutiveness of the adaptation reac­
tions and development of morphofunctional restructuring of the body.
The reason for such happenings is tied in with the changes in the external interactions of the 
body, a gradual increase in the intensity of the body work regime with an increase in sports mas­
tery and with changes tied in with these roles in the maintenance of separate functional systems, 
and likewise with a definite inertness of different body systems (Verkhoshansky, 13, 17, Yakov­
lev, 144 ).
There are three levels of adaptation restructuring, each of which has its own specific character in 
regard to heterochronicity of the accommodating restructuring and their corresponding physio­
logical processes and structural transformation (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, Verkhoshansky, 
Viru.28, 286 ).

They are:
level of biochemical processes ensuring energy and plastic functions at the time of work and 
immediately after its conclusion (level of quick homeostatic reactions); 
level of compensatory accommodation restructuring, in the foundation of which, are the 
structural (morphological) transformations in the body (level of compensatory adaptation); 
level of global functional-systemic restructuring (level of long term steady adaptation).
On the first level there are fast flowing biochemical processes activated in a definite consecu­
tiveness during work and post work periods (Figure 9).
In work, there is high excitation energy necessary for the muscle work and in the post work pe­
riod. liquidation of the biochemical changes that have taken place in the muscles and other or­
gans during the time of muscular work.
The most expressed changes are observed in energy exchange. In the muscle work there is a de­
crease in the content of the substrates for energy conversion (creatine phosphate, glycogen, and 
during long term work even the lipids) and an increase in the content of intercellular metabolism 
products.
The accumulation of these products and the stronger hormonal activity stimulates the oxidative 
processes in the tissues in the rest period after work. This serves to restore the intramuscular re­
serve of energy products, which leads to normalization of the water-electrolyte balance of the 
body and ensures the inductive synthesis of proteins in the organs that were subjected to the 
loads (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38).
The process of restoration, during the period of rest after muscular work, takes place at different 
speeds and ends at different times (Table 2).

Oxygen reserves and creatine phosphate in the working muscles are the fastest to recover fol­
lowed by inter muscular reserves of glycogen and liver glycogen and then the fat reserves that 
were used up during the protein structure work.
It is known that the intensity of the flow of the restorative processes, and the periods of filling 
the energy reserves in the body, depends upon the intensity and duration of their expenditure dur­
ing the time of muscular work (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38).
In the formation of compensatory accustomization restructuring, a definite consecutiveness in the 
improvement of physiological factors that determine the working effect of the motor functions 
can be clearly seen (Verkhoshansky 17, 24, 281- 284).
In a loaded work regime a shift in the 
functional characteristics of the body is 
observed first (Figure 10).
Intensification of this function acti­
vates a corresponding morphological 
(structural) restructuring (2), which, 
comes out as a quality material base 
for the adaptation process. This makes 
it possible to get further intensification 
of this function. Development of these 
mutually conditioning processes in 
turn, creates the prerequisites for rais­
ing the effect (power) of the external 
work of the body, which is reached by 
the more complete realization o f the 
motor potential of the body (Verkho­
shansky, 26, 27, 283, 284).
On the global level of the functional 
systemic restructuring of the body, development of adaptational changes are realized first of all 
because of the improved strength of the bio energetic processes. Following this is the bio energy 
volume and finally, improved bioenergetic effectiveness (economy) characterized by the level of 
use of the released energy into the metabolic processes for execution of specific muscle work.
In relation to separate bio energetic systems, the consecutiveness of development of adaptation 
during training takes on the following form: a faster increase in the capability of the aerobic oxi­
dative processes and maintenance of glycogen in the working muscles. Following this is mainte­
nance of the myofibril proteins (actin and myosin) and intensity of glycolosis. At the end, after 
everything - is maintenance of creatine phosphate (CP) and activeness of the creatine phos- 
phokinasis in the muscles (Margaria et al, 242, Yakovlev, 144, Volkov 38).
In this way, we get the greatest tempo of development and a longer period of maintaining a 
maximally high level that is characteristic for the biochemical indices of endurance for long term 
work, i.e., the aerobic abilities of the athlete. There is significantly slower development and 
shorter maintenance of a maximally high level of the biochemical indices of speed-strength 
qualities and speed endurance (Volkov, 38, Yakovlev, 144).
Several aspects of the heterochronicity phenomena of adaptation restructuring will be looked at 
further on in the section on laws of morphofunctional specialization of the athlete's body.

In the process of forming the behavioral adaptation reactions during strenuous muscle activity 
with complex motor coordination, attention is first given to the economically wasteful generali­
zation phase. This is seen in an abundance of extra movements in generally constrained move­
ments, motor system errors and a sharply expressed vegetative component (Bernstein. 7). Further 
on, according to the amount of skill formation and consolidation of extra movements in the mo­
tor system errors are eliminated and the vegetative component of the reaction is significantly de­
creased. In this way the end result becomes sufficient for maximum economy of the body re­
sources (Bernstein, 7, Farfel, 120, Verkhoshansky, 17, 25, 281, 281, Person, 95, 96, Donskoy, 
50, Granit, 210).
In this way, during successful adaptation to very different factors in the environment, high func­
tional economy appears to be a general characteristic trait of the systems, responsible for the ad­
aptation. This trait appears on different level of the system activity' as follows:
- 
on both the cellular and organ levels, where it is determined by the ratio of the different cel­
lular structures involved in the adaptive response;
on the level of the systems as a whole, where it is determined by the ratio of different or­
gans; and finally
on the level of neuro-humoral regulation, where economy appears as a consequence of 
greater reactiveness of the adapted organs to the mediator and hormone actions (Meerson, 
77, Viru, Kirge, 35, Haydarliu, 124).
One of the indicators of the athlete's adaptation to physical loads appears to be economy of the 
physiological systems functioning at rest and during moderate, sub-maximal loads. At the same 
time, during maximum loads, the body is capable of achieving a level of system functioning 
which is not possible by the untrained body (Farfel, 120, Pshennikova, 99). This feature is seen 
both within the limits of compensation as well as in the results of long term adaptation (Verkho­
shansky, Viru. 28. 286).
For example, the schematic on Figure 11 shows that doing low power work is easy for both the 
trained and untrained person, as differences in the physiological shifts (changes in energy expen­
diture, minute blood volume, breathing fre­
quency, etc.) are hardly seen. In more in­
tense work, in the untrained, a more sub­
stantial physiological shift takes place than

untrained, the functional shifts in them 
reach maximum, but in the trained they are 
still moderate, that is, for them this work is 
comparatively not hard.
The trained athlete can accomplish work
1.7. 
F u n ctio n al econom y o f the a d a p te d body
530

===== PDF 542 / p.531 =====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
with intensities that are significantly higher than those, wrhich for the untrained, appear to be 
maximal. In this, corresponding physiological shifts continue to increase. In the end, it reaches a 
limit work intensity and at this moment for the trained athletes it registers a maximum functional 
shift (Pshennicova, 99).
Means of economizing body functions during loaded muscle activity are extremely diverse and 
are determined by the functional specifics of the life ensuring systems of the body.
For example, in adaptation to loaded muscular activity requiring endurance, a significant in­
crease in the number of mitochondria in the skeletal muscles leads to a state that when at rest, or 
when the muscles are loaded, the portion of oxygen extracted from each liter of the flowing 
blood is greater than in the untrained body. As a result, an extreme increase in the minute volume 
of the heart during loaded activity shows up as being superfluous and ensures economy of blood 
circulation (Pshennikova, 99). Together with this, an increase in the strength of the mitochondrial 
system serves to increase the intensity of pyruvate utilization, decreasing its transition to lactate 
and consequently less accumulation of lactate in the muscles (Morgan et al., 250, Hollocszy, 
219, Riedy et al, 259).
In the end, the increased aerobic power of the body leads to an increase in its ability to utilize 
lipids to provide energy. The lipids have less of an energy effect in comparison to carbohydrates, 
but apparently they are used as a quality substrate for oxidation, sharply increasing the amount of 
energy as a consequence of their practically inexhaustible supply (Yakovlev, 140. Panin, 94, 
Haidarliu, 124) As a result, it allows for more economical use of glycogen during loaded activity 
(Holloszy et al, 224, Davies et al. 167, Galbo, 203).
The economic effect of adaptation of the body to physical loads on the level of the cardio­
vascular system has been given sufficient detailed study. The advantage of training the heart 
muscle together with changes in body adaptation, as a whole, ensures economic functioning of 
the heart at rest and during sub maximal physical loads. A decreased level of heart function at 
rest and a smaller functional increase during moderate loads, is conditioned in the trained body 
mainly by ncreased oxygen volume in the blood, increased ability of the tissues to extract oxygen 
from the blood (Yakovlev, 140, Astrand, Rodahl, 148) and greater micro circulation because of 
the widened capillary network in the skeletal muscles involved in fulfilling the main load, which 
makes it possible to increase the contact surface between the blood and muscle tissue.
Together with this, there is a decrease in the peripheral resistance of the vessels (Osoliny, 93). 
The main role in this is played by the formation of peripheral circulatory reactions that ensure 
effective redistribution of the blood flow and regulation of the oxygen entering into primarily the 
mobilized tissues and organs (Vasilieva, 11, Osoliny 93, Yankovsky, 146) and the stress on the 
anaerobic metabolites (Vasilieva, 11, Karlsson. 71, 232, Gollnik, Hermansen, 206). It is mainly 
these adaptive achievements that decrease the need for circulation and respiration in the body 
and make it possible to have normal provision of oxygen to the tissues and substrates with de­
creased minute blood volume.
The main role in the economy of functions of the trained heart, is played by the increased tension 
and speed of relaxation of the heart muscles (Meerson, Chashina, 79, Vasilieva, Stiopochkina,
10, De Maria et al., 188), and likewise the change in neuro-humoral regulation of the heart, de­
531

===== PDF 543 / p.532 =====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
veloped in the process of adaptation to the physical loads (Lin. Horvath. 237, Bolter, Gordon. 
158).
As a result of adaptation, there is an increase in the power and at the same time, economy of the 
motor system. Accommodation to the changes in the mechanisms directing muscular activity on 
the CNS level, leads to improvement of intra- and inter- muscular coordination, making it possi­
ble to mobilize a greater number of motor units during the loads and to synchronize their activity 
where strong concentrated effort is needed.
At the same time physical training leads to greater economy in the functioning of the neuromus­
cular system, and in the electrical activity of the skeletal muscles. There is an appreciable in­
crease in electrical activity in the muscles and fast development of fatigue is noticed in athletes 
during execution of the loads that are impossible for the untrained person (Yaschaninas, 147).
The main role in economy of energy in complex coordination motor actions is played by the se­
lection of the optimal, that is, more favorable movement due to the external strength and meta­
bolic energy generated by the body. Most frequently their interaction is accounted for by the 
formation of a so - called biodynamic structure, i.e., an expedient, steady means of tying together 
the accented moments of active and reactive dynamics in a movement system. With this, the lat­
ter becomes totally functionally oriented and specialized, and with this, responds to accommo­
date the external situation and the working mechanism for resolving motor tasks (Verkho­
shansky, 15, 19, 24, 25).
Finally, in a large group of sports (running, rowing, jumping, weightlifting), the active working 
effort is preceded by a sharp stretch of the muscles, whose elastic properties ensure accumulation 
of elastic (resilient) energy in the muscles. This energy provides economy to the movement sys­
tem as a whole (see reviews of the Author -18, 20).
In the process of forming steady, long term adaptation to physical loads, a restructuring takes 
place in the hormonal-humoral regulation of the functional systems involved in the adaptation 
(Yakovlev, 144, Viru, 32, 288, Meerson, 76, Viru, Kirge, 35, Pishniak, 100). In the adapted 
body, hormonal linked regulation functions more economically. In response to one and the same 
load in a trained body, there a significant decrease in the activation of the hormonal system to­
gether with correspondingly smaller increases in the concentration of hormones in the blood, 
than in the untrained body. This is accompanied by a limited stress reaction and absence of a 
negative, damaging component of this reaction, tied in with excessive “dispersal" of hormones 
(Meerson. 77, 78).
It is known that high intensity work is accompanied with expressed adrenaline. Raising body 
sensitivity to adrenaline, in the beginning stage of training, leads to extreme mobilization of en­
ergy sources during muscular activity. Together with this, according to the amount of increase in 
trainedness, the sensitivity of the tissues to the adrenaline decreases, this then produces a more 
economic distribution of the energy resources of the body (Yakovlev, 141, 142). It can be pro­
posed that this mechanism (decrease in the sensitivity of the tissues to adrenaline) conditions 
function economy, which ensures mobilization of respiration and glycolysis during execution of 
intensive loads (Pishniak, 100).
532

===== PDF 544 / p.533 =====
SUPERTRAINING ADDENDUM
The essentials of accommodative restructuring formation in the body during loaded muscular 
activity (adaptation inertness of individual physiological systems, herochronicity of their mor- 
pho-functional restructuring, specificity of adaptive protein synthesis, change in the role of sepa­
rate physiological systems and muscular groups, in development in body work power and speed 
of movement etc.) lead to the conclusion that there is some kind of optimal regime of develop­
ment of the adaptation process.
Such a regime should oversee a definite order and consecutiveness of development during the 
time of adaptation restructuring on different physiological body system levels, their interactions, 
tempo of development and amount of morpho-functional acquisition (Verkhoshansky, Viru, 
286).
During sports activity the process of adaptation (and consequently, the system of training) the 
end result is directed to increasing the power of work effort and speed of movement in a specific 
motor regime. The force of effort and speed of movement, is first of all an integral and important 
quality characteristic of the athlete’s mastery, and second, an important total result of the training 
process as a whole and third, - an important criterion of its effectiveness (Verkhoshansky, 24,25).
From here, in a formal relationship to the determined task and content of the training process, it 
is logical to assume that speed should be improved with speed work, and power- corresponding 
to the specifics of the intensity means. In order to develop strength it is necessary to use strength 
exercises, in order to increase speed it is necessary to execute speed work.
This is a natural path for improvement of sports mastery (Moreno, 94). Many coaches follow this 
outwardly non-controversial logic in practice (Verkhoshasky, 26).
For example, middle and long distance coaches are guided by the following principles:
- 
“if the main task is speed, then it follows that one should not get far away from it";
“speed achieved during the summer competitive season should be maintained during the 
following winter';
- 
“even during the winter, when training speed should not be ignored";
it is better to run 100 km a week with a specific speed load than to run 200km at a low inten­
sity” and so on. (Verkhoshasky, 26).
Analysis of the training methods in middle and long distance running shows that many coaches 
and runners who are led by such advice, begin to use intense interval and competitive runs even 
at the beginning of the preparatory period (Nurmekiwi, Piamat, 91).
In other words, from two alternative variants, increasing speed or power on the long stage of 
training (Figure 12,1) coaches usually select variant “A” and make a big mistake.
The problem is that the intensification of training in the preparatory period, which frequently in­
cludes execution of competitive exercises at high speed (power of effort), sharply raises the func­
tional abilities of the athlete and his competitive result. But, it does not create the morpho- 
functional base for further improving the specific work ability and sports progress. Because of 
this, such increases are insignificant and do not last very long (Figure 12, II, graphs “a" and “b"). 
More than this, premature high speed can show up as a negative influence on the flow of the 
training process.

In this way a contradictory situation is created: on the one side, speed requires high intensity

Methodological resolution of this contradiction in practical activity by the coach requires a high

One should not lean on speculative logic which can easily lead to the absurd as occurred in the

Nonetheless, speed work is necessary in training, as an important (specific) adaptogenic factor. 
However, speed work can become an effective means of specialized preparation only when the 
athlete is prepared for it. In other words, in order for the speed work to bring about a progressive 
shift in the body, it should be maximally high, but not so high that it would lead to an asthenic 
reaction in the body and interfere with the rational structure of movement. Because of this, 
maximally intense speed work should be approached gradually and not started earlier than the

activity of the cardio-vascular, respiratory and other body systems. In this, there is a decrease in

dystrophy and creates favourable conditions for peripheral circulatory reactions and adequate 
hemodynamics. Obviously, it is expedient to have an organization of training that oversees be­
ginning with an increase in heart volume and after this, increasing the power of its contractile 
function, which is achieved from an even greater increase in training load intensity. By the way, 
work with high intensity should not begin before the differentiated regional vessel reactions are 
firmly stabilized, that is, practically up to the precompetitive stage (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, 26, 
284, 285, 294, 295).

manner leads to further effective use of more intense means (Nyrmekivi, Piamat, 91).
If we take into consideration all of these arguments and laws of development of adaptation in 
general and in different motor regimes inherent in sports activities, then it is not difficult to come 
to the conclusion that the most favourable strategy of training is gradual intensification of the 
training work up to the moment of major starts (Figure 12, II graph “c”).
In speed-strength sports this allows for gradual preparation of the support-motor system for pow­
erful explosive efforts, and at the same time, improves the ability to execute the sports exercise 
with moderate intensity. In cyclical and team sports, work on optimal speed (on the anaerobic 
threshold level) and its increases, makes it possible to have level increases in the heart cavity 
volume and after this, myocardial power forming adequate peripheral vessel reactions and con­

The changes in the sports results and corresponding volumes of different intensity loads in both 
groups are presented in Figure 13, A and B.
It is easy to see that athletes using the intense preparation method (group B) had a higher result

of the main starts later on in the season, the athletes in group A came out on a higher level of 
sports preparation.
In this way, intensification of training in the preparatory period does not guarantee achieving 
high absolute results in the competitive period. With this thought in mind, the variant of training 
used by group A was more effective. But it is possible to come to the conclusion that the method 
of training in group A was more effective in preparing for the main meets of the season (as for 
example the Olympic games or World Championships) for showing the maximum possible (as 
for example, record breaking) results. Method B is more effective in those cases when a high 
performance level is required for during the entire yearly cycle of preparation (as for example in 
the Comrade games).
But this variant can be used only by athletes who are most highly qualified.

Consequently, in the preparatory period when training is directed mainly to the development of 
aerobic power, the use of such loads should be limited.
Here however, it is necessary to note that if a significant portion of time is devoted to execution 
of the sports events at a moderate speed, then at the moment of major competition there will 
simply not be enough time to adapt the body to the speed work regime. As a result they will not 
come out on the level of speed which is necessary for achievement of the planned for results. 
Besides this, in cyclical and team type sports, in each case, the muscle groups that carry the main 
load a will remain behind the vegetative systems according to tempo and level of functional im­
provement. As a consequence, it limits the increase in specialized workability of the athlete 
(Verkhoshansky, 24, 25).
In order to exclude these factors and to prepare the body for speed work without threat of its 
functional overload, it is expedient at the beginning of the big training cycle, when the competi­
tive exercises are executed at a moderate speed, to selectively intensify the motor system work 
regime with special physical (including strength) preparation. The exercises should be directed 
locally to those muscle groups that are mainly involved in competitive conditions. After this, ac­
cording to the amount of resolution of this task, it follows to use quality intensification of the 
competitive exercise by gradually increasing execution almost up to maximum speed.
Obviously, the coach intensifies the entire work regime of the body in conditions approaching 
the competitive.
But thanks to the preliminary morpho-functional preparation of the motor and other physiologi­
cal systems o f the body, this does not lead to its overload (more details on this concept and its 
practical uses are available in various studies (Verkhoshansky, 25, 284, 285 Verkhoshansky, 
Zaleev, 29).

A. Means (loads) ensuring morpho-functional specialization of the body as a whole and primar­
ily the locomotor system in correspondence with the specific competitive activity - task of get­
ting ahead with the body preparation for speed work (Verkhoshansky, 26, 27, 284, 285).
B. Means (loads) directed to the intensification of the motor regime, using primarily the competi­
tive exercise.
C. Competition activities (loads) writh the increasing of speed.
All of what has been said above about the optimal regime of development of the adaptational 
process in the yearly cycle, relates fully to multiyear training. Premature intensification and 
preparation of young athletes does not create favourable conditions for progress in their future 
mastery.
For example, it has been shown that in the preparation of sprinters, Soviet coaches for many 
years were oriented not to creating a solid foundation for achieving high level results, but to fast 
tempo increases in achievement based on narrow specialized means. This led to early mobiliza­
tion of reserves possessed by young athletes which exhausted their capabilities and as a result, at

The phenomena of decreasing of immunological reactivity
It has long been known that extreme physical and psycho-emotional loads in contemporary sport 
have a depressing influence on the defense systems of the body (Kassil et al, 61, Surkina et al.

a) 
increasing imbalance in the humerol-hormonal regulatory function during intense sports 
loads;
b) 
exhaustion of the sympathoadrenal system and hypophyseal-adrenocortical hystem;
c) 
progressive increases in activeness of the trophotropic mechanisms;
d) 
accompanied increases in tonus of the centrally formed parasympathetic section of the 
vegetative (autonomic) nervous system;
e) 
increased permeability of the Hematoencephalic barrier 17 for several hormones and;

deep metabolic changes arising in the middle of the mix (Levando et al., 70, Suzdalnitzky 
et al. 108).
Depressed immunologic reactiveness is tied in with increased inflection-inflammation illnesses 
of the athlete when using large training loads and when competing in major competitions. Many 
instances have been observed which give evidence to the fact that at the peak of trainedness in 
weightlifters, wrestlers and other athletes, there is frequently observed a decrease in resistance to 
the influence of cold and cold type illness (Meerson, Pshennikova, 78).
It has been established (Aronov et al, 2) that in many high level athletes (rowers) training and 
competitive loads lead to a decrease in immune reactiveness, and its recovery takes place very 
slowly. This is tied in with inadequately high intensity of the loads used. Analogous observa­
tions have been seen in studies of the physiology of children's sport (Suharev, Suhanova, 110, 
Prasdnikov, 98). It has been shown that an optimal training load in young athletes increases the 
immunological reactivenss in comparison to children not participating in sport. But, during in­
tense loads, the immune-reactiveness of children decreases (Suharev, Suhanova, 110).
In the “sports form” state there is a sharp increase in the number of acute and chronic illnesses. 
If illness in athletes before beginning the training year with moderate intensity loads is 1, then in 
the competitive period tied in with intensified trainings, it increases 5-10 times, and immediately 
before competition up to 25 times (Levando, 76). It is known that on the day before and during

The process of adaptation is determined principally by the following components:
A) 
Biosynthesis;
B) 
Internal factors;
C) 
Mechanisms of their interactions (Kaznacheev, 59).
In evaluating any of these components, it is necessary to consider the properties of a single pur­
pose biosystem (aim of system control) and conditions (situations) to overcome, which the body 
requires in adaptation.
Multiple studies have produced a store of scientific knowledge on the theory of adaptation. Ex­
amined (studied) were the essentials of adaptation of man to extreme conditions of his surround­
ings, both social and native, and frequently climatic-geographic factors, artificially changing the 
surrounding conditions, change in the geographical zone and changes in the daily dynamics of 
the functions, of one or several factors, the form of fractional, continuous and cross sectional ad­
aptation and so on.
Characteristic for all of these conditions are the specific essentials of the general laws of devel­
opment of the adaptational process and the mechanisms of their realization.
The content and structure of the general theory of adaptation is sufficiently complex (and it 
should be noted, insufficiently regulated). Because of this, in order to not remain on the ascer­
tained or declarative level; the essence of which contains unsubstantiated, non-constructive dis­
cussion and conclusions, it follows to describe completely, the specifics of the adaptational proc­
ess and the essentials for realization of the adaptational mechanism during sports activity. This 
is all the more necessary7 in order to determine the place for presenting the specific essentials of 
the adaptational process in sport, within the limits of general adaptation, and to effectively use its 
principal position in interpreting literary and original experimental data.

After this, it decreases to the beginning level (and even somewhat lower), and a new but already smaller increase above the initial levels and finally, establishment of the level which existed before work (Yakovlev, 144)." Fig 6 ("The process of the energy supplying during muscular activity (I) and the rest (II) according to Jiakovlev, 1988"; the caption spells the name so, the text spells it Yakovlev) draws one curve over a horizontal baseline: it falls through phase I (labelled "Work"), bottoms at the dashed line that divides I from II, climbs back through phase II ("Recovery"), peaks well above the baseline, falls to just under it, and ends in a small hump. The caption numbers the parts "1- consummation, 2 - restitution, 3 - super compensation, 4 - the wave form returning to the initial level." The y-axis is "the level of the energy sources"; neither axis has a scale or unit.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The page gives a dose rule, not a mechanism: "the amount of super-compensation and the speed of its appearance, is directly related to the intensity of the expended products during the time of work, and the duration of maintaining this phase, from the absolute amounts of expenditure range from several hours to 1-2 days)" (PDF 534 / p.523; the parenthesis is unbalanced on the page). Its consequence: "after work, during the time of rest, not only is the pre-work state of the muscles restored (and the body as a whole) but for some period, conditions for increased workability are created." And: "The phase of supercompensation appears as a first step in adaptation of the body to muscular activity (Yakovlev, 138). Regardless of its short term (from several hours to 2-3 days), it is ensures execution of the following loads in conditions that are more favorable to the body" (same page).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — As the classic one-factor picture of a single session's after-effect, when a coach asks why the next hard session should fall on a recovered rather than a depleted state. Inference: the wave shape in Fig 6 implies that a window above baseline is followed by a second, smaller dip, so "later" is not always "better" for the next load; the page does not give times for the dip.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Yakovlev is cited (138, 144) but no study, population, load or data is described, and Fig 6 is an unscaled schematic. The same page gives two durations for the phase: "several hours to 1-2 days" and, three sentences later, "several hours to 2-3 days" (PDF 534 / p.523); quote whichever you use with its sentence. Within this book the claim is not settled. The next paragraph extends the "law of supercompensation" to "creatine phosphate, the enzymatic and structural proteins, to the phosolipids, and to a number of mitochondria in the muscle fibers - in a word, for all products and structures, which to one or another degree, were expended or destroyed" (PDF 534 / p.523), while the 1.16 text states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (PDF 99 / p.88). That contest is already recorded in [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] and [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]; this entry does not reopen it. Inference: glycogen is the one substance both passages accept as overshooting, so the Fig 6 example is the least disputed part of the section.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: glycogen falls in work, rises above its initial level in rest, drops to or below that level, rises a little above it again, and then settles at the pre-work level (Yakovlev, 144; Fig 6, PDF 534 / p.523).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16, the book's own reservation), [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1, supercompensation as the short level), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]] (9.1, the same depress-then-overshoot shape for protein synthesis), [[claim--restitution-scales-with-work-expenditure-and-sets-adaptive-biosynthesis]], [[claim--trainedness-is-the-sum-of-session-after-effects-and-lowers-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]

    14	# Trainedness Is the Summed After-Effect of Increasing Loads, and a Trained Body Is Disturbed Less by the Same Work
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 534-535 / pp.523-524, checked against the page images): "In systematic execution of increasing loads, the after effects left by each of them are summed up, leading to stable adaptation of the body, a state of trainedness. A more general form of the latter (from a biochemical position) is characterized by an increase in the energy potential of the body and ability to use it in restoration. In the base of this is the increased activity of many enzymatic systems accommodating changes in the regulation of the metabolic processes, and likewise, maintaining homeostasis." The result: "the emerging adaptational changes from the muscular activity lead to fewer disturbances of the ATP balance and less disturbance of homeostasis in the trained body. In execution of these loads, according to their intensity or duration close to the limit (which, under the influence of training constantly moves further out) the trained body can withstand disturbances of homeostasis more easily. All of this ensures the ability to execute work at a given intensity longer, that is, greater endurance" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The stated basis is enzymatic: more active enzyme systems regulate metabolism and hold homeostasis, so a given load costs the ATP balance less (PDF 534-535). No study or data is given for this paragraph.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When explaining why the same session feels and measures easier as a block goes on, and why the ceiling of tolerable load rises with training. Inference: the claim pairs with the 1.7 economy argument later in 9.1 ([[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]]): less disturbance at a fixed load, and a higher limit.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: the paragraph cites no study and shows no data; it is a summary statement. "Summed up" after-effects assume each load lands while the last one's effect is still present; the page does not say how close together loads must be. Inference: a falling disturbance at a fixed load is also what a load that has become too easy looks like, so it argues for raising the load, which the page builds in ("increasing loads"), not for holding it.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own conclusion: the trained body can withstand disturbances of homeostasis "more easily," which "ensures the ability to execute work at a given intensity longer, that is, greater endurance" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]], [[claim--restitution-scales-with-work-expenditure-and-sets-adaptive-biosynthesis]], [[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]], [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]]

    13	
    14	# The Bigger the Expenditure and Breakdown in Work, the Bigger the Restitution That Follows
    15	
    16	**What it is** — 9a recorded that one of the three bases of the constructive effect of adaptation is "a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work" (PDF 530 / p.519). On PDF 535 / p.524 Verkhoshansky spells out what it means (checked against the page image): "The intensity of the biochemical restitution in the after-work period, the same as the expressed phases of supercompensation of the maintained sources for movement, is spread out over the time of muscular activity, and positively correlates with the intensity of their dispersion. The greater the energy expenditure and breakdown of protein structures in the process of work, then to the greatest extent, will be the recovery that follows." He then ties it to adaptation: "the biochemical shifts in the muscle fibers brought out by the muscular activity, determines the following phasic changes in their energy exchange and the increase in the energy balance in the after-work period that appears initially for activation of the adaptational biosynthesis (Yakovlev, 143)." In 1.6 he repeats the rule for refilling stores: "the intensity of the flow of the restorative processes, and the periods of filling the energy reserves in the body, depends upon the intensity and duration of their expenditure during the time of muscular work (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38)" (PDF 540 / p.529).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The page's logic: the work shifts set the programme that the rest period carries out, so the size of the after-work response follows the size of the shift (PDF 535). The translation is rough ("spread out over the time of muscular activity," "intensity of their dispersion"); Inference: "dispersion" most likely means expenditure.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a coach wants a reason that a light session produces a small adaptive response, not just a small fatigue cost. Inference: it is the session-level version of the stage-level rule in [[heuristic--restorative-stage-length-scales-with-homeostatic-disturbance]]: more disturbance, more restoration needed and more rebound available.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Yakovlev and Volkov are cited without any study described. The rule is stated without an upper limit on this page. Inference: read without one, "the greater the expenditure, the greater the recovery" invites overload; 9.1 itself sets the limit elsewhere: "Extreme intensification of training leads to depression of the catabolic and anabolic stages of the general adaptation reaction" and limits "the super-compensation of carbohydrate and plastic reserves" (PDF 545 / p.534; see [[claim--premature-intensification-harms-heart-mitochondria-and-support-motor-system]]).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own wording of the rule: "The greater the energy expenditure and breakdown of protein structures in the process of work, then to the greatest extent, will be the recovery that follows" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1, the third basis of the constructive effect), [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]], [[claim--trainedness-is-the-sum-of-session-after-effects-and-lowers-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[heuristic--restorative-stage-length-scales-with-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--premature-intensification-harms-heart-mitochondria-and-support-motor-system]]

    14	# Verkhoshansky Extends the Supercompensation Law From the Session to Concentrated Training Stages of 10-12 Weeks
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 535 / p.524, checked against the page image): "Many complex studies (see the revues of 24 and 25) have convincingly shown that the laws of supercompensation of products and energy applies not only in short term muscular work but also to conditions of prolonged training as for example, when using methodological methods of concentrating SPP (specialized physical preparation) loads on time limited stages (10-12 weeks)." The studies were "directed to studying the capabilities of rationalizing the training in the yearly cycle," in "track and field running (Levchenko. 71, Dubinin, 51, Narskin. 87, Vrublevsky, 39) and jumping (Antonova. 1, Mironenko, 82, Nikitin, 88, Dushenkov 52. Umarov, 117) volleyball (Naraliev. 86), tennis (Verkhoshansky, 12), rowing (Turcheniuk. 114), judo (Koptev, 64), weightlifting (Ganchenko 40), and others." The finding: "there is a long decrease in the functional abilities of athletes during periods (or stages) of using concentrated (that is. concentrated in a limited time period) strength loads. After concluding the strength loads all the functional indices not only return to the initial level but substantially go above it (Figure 7). This phenomenon received the name of long term delayed training effect (LDTE)" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's framing: the LDTE is the same law as the session overshoot ([[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]]), acting over weeks. Inference: this sentence states the link between the two levels that [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] records as unstated on PDF 530; it is still an assertion, since no mechanism for the long level is given here.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When placing a concentrated strength or SPP block in the year and explaining to staff why the athlete will be flat during it. The list of sports gives the range the author claims: running, jumping, volleyball, tennis, rowing, judo, weightlifting.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: the page says the studies "convincingly" showed it but describes none of them (no populations, loads or data). Two durations sit a page apart: concentrated SPP stages of "10-12 weeks" here (PDF 535 / p.524) and, in the next list, "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks" (PDF 536 / p.525). Keep each number with its locator. The loads in every case are "strength loads" or SPP, including in running and rowing. Inference: this is not evidence of an LDTE after aerobic or distance loading, which Chapter 6 says is documented only after altitude training ([[claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training]]); the two passages describe different loads, so they are not in conflict. Calling the LDTE "supercompensation" also inherits the book's internal dispute over that word ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own sport list for the finding, from running and jumping to weightlifting and judo (PDF 535 / p.524). The 9.1 restatement of the LDTE rules and Fig 7 is recorded on [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]; the triple-jump case he gives with them is [[case-study--triple-jumper-annual-cycle-two-strength-blocks-fig-8]].
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (6.10), [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[case-study--triple-jumper-annual-cycle-two-strength-blocks-fig-8]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]

    14	# One Triple Jumper's Year (Fig 8): Two Concentrated Strength-and-Bounding Blocks, Each Followed by a Rise in Strength and Jump Results
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky gives Fig 8 as his example of the LDTE (9.1 §1.5, PDF 536 / p.525 text, PDF 537 / p.526 figure; figure read from a 300 dpi render of the page image). The caption: "Dynamics of the speed-strength parameters, the volumes of the carried out training loads and the sport results of the triple jumper during the yearly cycle (from October - to August)." Top panel: monthly "P0, maximal strength," "Fmax, magnitude of the maximal explosive effort," and "Jd., index of explosive strength," on a left axis in "Kg" (160 to 200) and a right axis in "Kg/sec" (350 to 550); the figure does not say which line uses which axis. Middle panel: triple-jump result in m. Bottom panel: monthly "barbell exercises (in tones - on the left axe)," "bounds" in km on the right axis, and "the whole competition exercises executions (number of repetitions - on the left axe)." Approximate readings from the image (months X to VIII):
    17	- Barbell, tonnes: 35, 75, 16, 14, 1, 75, 58, 19, 4, 16, 2.
    18	- Bounds, km: 7.3, 9.3, 1.8, 0.4, 1.0, 8.6, 5.0, 0.5, 0.6, 1.0, 0.6.
    19	- Triple jumps, repetitions: 20, 34, 73, 44, 20, 36, 95, 60, 40, 50, 30.
    20	- P0, kg: 170, 172, 178, 192, 190, 183, 192, 194, 200, 196, 200.
    21	- Fmax and Jd, read on the left scale: Fmax about 166 to 188, dipping in III and VII; Jd about 165, 161, 168, 173, 175, 164, 160, 172, 174, 169, 177, its low point in IV.
    22	- Triple jump, m (plotted from XII): 15.96, 16.22, 16.06, 16.04, 16.02, 16.46, 16.30, 15.98, 16.50.
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's reading (PDF 536 / p.525): "after the concentrated specialized strength preparation loads in March-April, the LDTE acquired showed an increase in speed-strength and increased sports results in May-June. [H]owever, an insignificant increase in their volume in specialized strength preparation (by only a [f]ew percent) in order to 'maintain' the achieved level of specialized workability (as believed by [t]he athlete) led to a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results. As a result of this, the ath[l]ete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team." This quote is partly reconstructed: the left margin of the page is clipped in the scan, so the bracketed letters are missing on the page image. He uses it to illustrate his point 6: in the LDTE period "volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily ... but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (same page).
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — As a worked picture of what the dip and rebound look like in one athlete's monthly numbers, when planning where a concentrated strength block ends relative to the main competitions. Inference: the figure shows the pattern twice, not once. A first block in X-XI (barbell 75 t and bounds 9.3 km in XI) is followed by P0 and the jump rising to a winter peak in I (192 kg, 16.22 m); the second block in III-IV (75 t and 8.6 km in III) is followed by the May-June peak the text names. The text mentions only March-April.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — One athlete, readings by eye, and no statistics, so `supported` here means a described case with printed data, not a tested rule. Three mismatches between text and figure: the text says "in triple jumpers" (plural) while the caption and the rest of the passage are singular; the text says the strength volume rose "by only a few percent," but the figure's barbell volume goes from about 4 t in VI to about 16 t in VII and bounds from about 0.6 to 1.0 km (Inference: that is a large relative rise from a small base, so the "few percent" may mean a share of total volume; the page does not say); and the August rebound to about 16.50 m, the best mark in the figure, is not discussed. Jump repetitions also rose from VI to VII (about 40 to 50), so the July drop cannot be laid on strength volume alone (Inference). Point 6 itself reads the other way round from Chapter 6, which is recorded as a contest in [[heuristic--time-technique-and-competition-strength-work-to-the-ldte-window]].
    29	
    30	**Example** — From the figure: in III the barbell volume is about 75 t and bounds about 8.6 km, Jd falls to its low in IV, and in V the jump rises from about 16.02 m to about 16.46 m with barbell volume cut to about 19 t (PDF 537 / p.526, approximate image readings).

    14	# Adaptation Is Heterochronic and Runs on Three Levels: Quick Homeostatic Reactions, Compensatory Structural Change, Long-Term Systemic Restructuring
    15	
    16	**What it is** — 9.1 §1.6, "Heterochronism of the adaptational restructuring" (PDF 538 / p.527, checked against the page image). Verkhoshansky: "Development of the adaptation process is tied in with a definite heterochronicity in the formation of accommodative body restructuring. Heterochronicity appears first in the failure to coincide moments of time with the corresponding beginnings of the intense improvement of one or another functional system. Second, it appears in the specific consecutiveness of the adaptation reactions and development of morphofunctional restructuring of the body." The three levels, each with "its own specific character in regard to heterochronicity" (PDF 538-539 / pp.527-528):
    17	1. "level of biochemical processes ensuring energy and plastic functions at the time of work and immediately after its conclusion (level of quick homeostatic reactions)";
    18	2. "level of compensatory accommodation restructuring, in the foundation of which, are the structural (morphological) transformations in the body (level of compensatory adaptation)";
    19	3. "level of global functional-systemic restructuring (level of long term steady adaptation)."
    20	The first level is detailed by Fig 9 and Table 2 ([[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]); the second and third by Fig 10 ([[claim--function-leads-structure-and-power-precedes-capacity-and-economy-fig-10]]).
    21	
    22	**Why it works** — The stated causes of heterochronicity: "the changes in the external interactions of the body, a gradual increase in the intensity of the body work regime with an increase in sports mastery and with changes tied in with these roles in the maintenance of separate functional systems, and likewise with a definite inertness of different body systems (Verkhoshansky, 13, 17, Yakovlev, 144)" (PDF 538 / p.527).
    23	
    24	**When to apply** — When reading a monitoring trend: a fast marker (a session's metabolic response) and a slow one (structural or whole-system change) are expected to move at different times, so a lack of change in a slow marker after a few weeks is not by itself a failed block. Inference: the three levels map onto session, block and multi-year time scales; the page names the levels but gives no durations for them.
    25	
    26	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a conceptual scheme with citations (Verkhoshansky 24, 25; Verkhoshansky and Viru 28, 286) and no data. The same three levels reappear as the opening of 1.10 on PDF 554 (outside this batch); 9a's Viru scheme ([[framework--viru-general-adaptation-mechanism-specific-homeostatic-vs-general-fig-2]]) is a related but separate sequence (specific, general, long-term). The page says more on heterochronicity is in "the section on laws of morphofunctional specialization" (PDF 540 / p.529), which is outside this batch.
    27	
    28	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own level 1: "fast flowing biochemical processes activated in a definite consecutiveness during work and post work periods (Figure 9)" (PDF 539 / p.528).

Work, from the bottom: "Muscular activity" leads to "Demolition of ATP," then "Changing in the ATP balance," then "Accumulation of metabolites." Two side paths feed in: "Consumption of glycogen and fat acids" leads to "Partial ATP re-synthesis," which feeds the ATP-balance box; and "Muscular activity" leads to "Oxygen deficit (working hypoxia)," which feeds "Accumulation of metabolites." Recovery, from the line upward: "Oxygenation of metabolites," "Increase in the ATP production," "Super compensation of CP and glycogen contents," "Synthesis of proteins." A side arrow also runs from "Increase in the ATP production" straight to "Synthesis of proteins." The text (PDF 539 / p.528, checked against the page image): in work, substrates fall ("creatine phosphate, glycogen, and during long term work even the lipids") and metabolism products rise; "The accumulation of these products and the stronger hormonal activity stimulates the oxidative processes in the tissues in the rest period after work. This serves to restore the intramuscular reserve of energy products, which leads to normalization of the water-electrolyte balance of the body and ensures the inductive synthesis of proteins in the organs that were subjected to the loads (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38)."
190	    17	
191	    18	**Why it works** — In the scheme, the metabolites made in work are the trigger for the recovery chain: they drive oxidation, which powers the restoration of energy stores and then protein synthesis. Inference: this is the same metabolite-as-inducer idea 9a recorded ([[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]), drawn as a sequence.
192	    19	
193	    20	**When to apply** — As the first-level picture in [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]], when explaining why protein synthesis comes last in recovery, after energy stores. Inference: it supports the 9a caution that clearing metabolites during rest may blunt the later steps ([[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]]).
194	    21	
195	    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: a flow chart credited to Yakovlev (1986) with no data or timings; the times are in Table 2 ([[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]). The box "Super compensation of CP and glycogen contents" asserts CP supercompensation, which the 1.16 text does not accept ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]).
196	    23	
197	    24	**Example** — The figure's recovery column in order: oxygenation of metabolites, increased ATP production, supercompensation of CP and glycogen, synthesis of proteins (PDF 538 / p.527).
198	    25	
199	    26	**Related** — [[framework--heterochronism-and-three-levels-of-adaptation-restructuring]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--clearing-metabolites-during-rest-blunts-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]

214	    14	# Restoration Times After Loaded Work, Process by Process (Table 2, Volkov 1986 and Fox 1981): Minutes for Phosphagens, Hours for Lactate and Glycogen, Up to 72 Hours for Protein Synthesis
215	    15	
216	    16	**What it is** — "The process of restoration, during the period of rest after muscular work, takes place at different speeds and ends at different times (Table 2)" (9.1 §1.6, PDF 539 / p.528). Table 2, "Time necessary for restoration of different biochemical processes in the period of rest after loaded muscle work (According to N. Volkov, 1986 and E. Fox, 1981)," as printed (checked against the page image), in the printed order:
217	    17	- "Restoration of the phosphogens in the muscles (ATP and CP)": from 2-3 min.
218	    18	- "Restoration of oxygen reserves in the body": from 10-15 sec.
219	    19	- "Payback/recovery of alactic oxygen debt": from 3-5 min.
220	    20	- "Clearance of lactic acid": active rest from 30 min to 1 hour; passive rest from 1-2 hr.
221	    21	- "Restoration of inter muscular reserves of glycogen": after long term work from 10-46 hours; after non long term work from 5-24 hours.
222	    22	- "Restoration of glycogen reserves in the liver": from 12-48 hours.
223	    23	- "Strengthening of inductive synthesis of enzyme and structural proteins": from 12-72 hours.
224	    24	
225	    25	**Why it works** — The text's ordering (PDF 540 / p.529): "Oxygen reserves and creatine phosphate in the working muscles are the fastest to recover followed by inter muscular reserves of glycogen and liver glycogen and then the fat reserves that were used up during the protein structure work." The time depends on the dose: restoration "depends upon the intensity and duration of their expenditure during the time of muscular work" (same page). Inference: "inter muscular" is almost certainly intramuscular (the PDF 539 text says "intramuscular reserve"), and the fat-reserves clause is garbled in translation.

Eric's baseline: "Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 153, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)). Inference: a table of this kind is a load-design tool that fits that practice.

The table lists oxygen reserves (10-15 sec) after phosphagens (2-3 min) though it is the faster process; quote the printed order. The text's order puts fat reserves last, while the table's last and longest row is protein synthesis; fats are not in the table. The 12-72 hour protein-synthesis row should be read with Fig 5 in 9a, whose curves stay above baseline far longer ([[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]]).

    12	---
    13	
    14	# After Work, Glycogen Does Not Just Return to Baseline: It Overshoots, Dips Below, Overshoots Less, Then Settles (Yakovlev, Fig 6)
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In 9.1 §1.5, after the Meerson paragraph that closes 9a, Verkhoshansky goes back to Yakovlev's earlier work (PDF 534 / p.523, checked against the page image): "Even before this it had been shown that in the process of physical work, the biochemical shifts that take place in the body during the period of rest become normalized, going through a series of phases which include the phase of supercompensation of those ingredients that were expended. This pertains to the substrates serving as sources of energy as well as the different structural and enzymatic proteins (Yakovlev, 138)." His example is glycogen, which "during the time of rest, increases not only to the initial, but to a higher level (Figure 6). After this, it decreases to the beginning level (and even somewhat lower), and a new but already smaller increase above the initial levels and finally, establishment of the level which existed before work (Yakovlev, 144)." Fig 6 ("The process of the energy supplying during muscular activity (I) and the rest (II) according to Jiakovlev, 1988"; the caption spells the name so, the text spells it Yakovlev) draws one curve over a horizontal baseline: it falls through phase I (labelled "Work"), bottoms at the dashed line that divides I from II, climbs back through phase II ("Recovery"), peaks well above the baseline, falls to just under it, and ends in a small hump. The caption numbers the parts "1- consummation, 2 - restitution, 3 - super compensation, 4 - the wave form returning to the initial level." The y-axis is "the level of the energy sources"; neither axis has a scale or unit.
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The page gives a dose rule, not a mechanism: "the amount of super-compensation and the speed of its appearance, is directly related to the intensity of the expended products during the time of work, and the duration of maintaining this phase, from the absolute amounts of expenditure range from several hours to 1-2 days)" (PDF 534 / p.523; the parenthesis is unbalanced on the page). Its consequence: "after work, during the time of rest, not only is the pre-work state of the muscles restored (and the body as a whole) but for some period, conditions for increased workability are created." And: "The phase of supercompensation appears as a first step in adaptation of the body to muscular activity (Yakovlev, 138). Regardless of its short term (from several hours to 2-3 days), it is ensures execution of the following loads in conditions that are more favorable to the body" (same page).
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — As the classic one-factor picture of a single session's after-effect, when a coach asks why the next hard session should fall on a recovered rather than a depleted state. Inference: the wave shape in Fig 6 implies that a window above baseline is followed by a second, smaller dip, so "later" is not always "better" for the next load; the page does not give times for the dip.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Yakovlev is cited (138, 144) but no study, population, load or data is described, and Fig 6 is an unscaled schematic. The same page gives two durations for the phase: "several hours to 1-2 days" and, three sentences later, "several hours to 2-3 days" (PDF 534 / p.523); quote whichever you use with its sentence. Within this book the claim is not settled. The next paragraph extends the "law of supercompensation" to "creatine phosphate, the enzymatic and structural proteins, to the phosolipids, and to a number of mitochondria in the muscle fibers - in a word, for all products and structures, which to one or another degree, were expended or destroyed" (PDF 534 / p.523), while the 1.16 text states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" (PDF 99 / p.88). That contest is already recorded in [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] and [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]]; this entry does not reopen it. Inference: glycogen is the one substance both passages accept as overshooting, so the Fig 6 example is the least disputed part of the section.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: glycogen falls in work, rises above its initial level in rest, drops to or below that level, rises a little above it again, and then settles at the pre-work level (Yakovlev, 144; Fig 6, PDF 534 / p.523).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]] (1.16, the book's own reservation), [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1, supercompensation as the short level), [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]] (9.1, the same depress-then-overshoot shape for protein synthesis), [[claim--restitution-scales-with-work-expenditure-and-sets-adaptive-biosynthesis]], [[claim--trainedness-is-the-sum-of-session-after-effects-and-lowers-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[framework--restoration-times-by-biochemical-process-table-2]]

    13	
    14	# Trainedness Is the Summed After-Effect of Increasing Loads, and a Trained Body Is Disturbed Less by the Same Work
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 534-535 / pp.523-524, checked against the page images): "In systematic execution of increasing loads, the after effects left by each of them are summed up, leading to stable adaptation of the body, a state of trainedness. A more general form of the latter (from a biochemical position) is characterized by an increase in the energy potential of the body and ability to use it in restoration. In the base of this is the increased activity of many enzymatic systems accommodating changes in the regulation of the metabolic processes, and likewise, maintaining homeostasis." The result: "the emerging adaptational changes from the muscular activity lead to fewer disturbances of the ATP balance and less disturbance of homeostasis in the trained body. In execution of these loads, according to their intensity or duration close to the limit (which, under the influence of training constantly moves further out) the trained body can withstand disturbances of homeostasis more easily. All of this ensures the ability to execute work at a given intensity longer, that is, greater endurance" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The stated basis is enzymatic: more active enzyme systems regulate metabolism and hold homeostasis, so a given load costs the ATP balance less (PDF 534-535). No study or data is given for this paragraph.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When explaining why the same session feels and measures easier as a block goes on, and why the ceiling of tolerable load rises with training. Inference: the claim pairs with the 1.7 economy argument later in 9.1 ([[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]]): less disturbance at a fixed load, and a higher limit.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: the paragraph cites no study and shows no data; it is a summary statement. "Summed up" after-effects assume each load lands while the last one's effect is still present; the page does not say how close together loads must be. Inference: a falling disturbance at a fixed load is also what a load that has become too easy looks like, so it argues for raising the load, which the page builds in ("increasing loads"), not for holding it.
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own conclusion: the trained body can withstand disturbances of homeostasis "more easily," which "ensures the ability to execute work at a given intensity longer, that is, greater endurance" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]], [[claim--restitution-scales-with-work-expenditure-and-sets-adaptive-biosynthesis]], [[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]], [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[principle--loading-volume-disturbs-homeostasis-and-prepares-connective-tissue]]

    13	
    14	# The Bigger the Expenditure and Breakdown in Work, the Bigger the Restitution That Follows
    15	
    16	**What it is** — 9a recorded that one of the three bases of the constructive effect of adaptation is "a positive correlation between the catabolic and anabolic processes, brought about by the muscular work" (PDF 530 / p.519). On PDF 535 / p.524 Verkhoshansky spells out what it means (checked against the page image): "The intensity of the biochemical restitution in the after-work period, the same as the expressed phases of supercompensation of the maintained sources for movement, is spread out over the time of muscular activity, and positively correlates with the intensity of their dispersion. The greater the energy expenditure and breakdown of protein structures in the process of work, then to the greatest extent, will be the recovery that follows." He then ties it to adaptation: "the biochemical shifts in the muscle fibers brought out by the muscular activity, determines the following phasic changes in their energy exchange and the increase in the energy balance in the after-work period that appears initially for activation of the adaptational biosynthesis (Yakovlev, 143)." In 1.6 he repeats the rule for refilling stores: "the intensity of the flow of the restorative processes, and the periods of filling the energy reserves in the body, depends upon the intensity and duration of their expenditure during the time of muscular work (Yakovlev, 141, 142, 144, Volkov, 38)" (PDF 540 / p.529).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The page's logic: the work shifts set the programme that the rest period carries out, so the size of the after-work response follows the size of the shift (PDF 535). The translation is rough ("spread out over the time of muscular activity," "intensity of their dispersion"); Inference: "dispersion" most likely means expenditure.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When a coach wants a reason that a light session produces a small adaptive response, not just a small fatigue cost. Inference: it is the session-level version of the stage-level rule in [[heuristic--restorative-stage-length-scales-with-homeostatic-disturbance]]: more disturbance, more restoration needed and more rebound available.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Yakovlev and Volkov are cited without any study described. The rule is stated without an upper limit on this page. Inference: read without one, "the greater the expenditure, the greater the recovery" invites overload; 9.1 itself sets the limit elsewhere: "Extreme intensification of training leads to depression of the catabolic and anabolic stages of the general adaptation reaction" and limits "the super-compensation of carbohydrate and plastic reserves" (PDF 545 / p.534; see [[claim--premature-intensification-harms-heart-mitochondria-and-support-motor-system]]).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own wording of the rule: "The greater the energy expenditure and breakdown of protein structures in the process of work, then to the greatest extent, will be the recovery that follows" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] (9.1, the third basis of the constructive effect), [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]], [[claim--trainedness-is-the-sum-of-session-after-effects-and-lowers-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[heuristic--restorative-stage-length-scales-with-homeostatic-disturbance]], [[claim--metabolites-induce-and-hormones-amplify-adaptive-protein-synthesis]], [[claim--premature-intensification-harms-heart-mitochondria-and-support-motor-system]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Verkhoshansky Extends the Supercompensation Law From the Session to Concentrated Training Stages of 10-12 Weeks
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.5, PDF 535 / p.524, checked against the page image): "Many complex studies (see the revues of 24 and 25) have convincingly shown that the laws of supercompensation of products and energy applies not only in short term muscular work but also to conditions of prolonged training as for example, when using methodological methods of concentrating SPP (specialized physical preparation) loads on time limited stages (10-12 weeks)." The studies were "directed to studying the capabilities of rationalizing the training in the yearly cycle," in "track and field running (Levchenko. 71, Dubinin, 51, Narskin. 87, Vrublevsky, 39) and jumping (Antonova. 1, Mironenko, 82, Nikitin, 88, Dushenkov 52. Umarov, 117) volleyball (Naraliev. 86), tennis (Verkhoshansky, 12), rowing (Turcheniuk. 114), judo (Koptev, 64), weightlifting (Ganchenko 40), and others." The finding: "there is a long decrease in the functional abilities of athletes during periods (or stages) of using concentrated (that is. concentrated in a limited time period) strength loads. After concluding the strength loads all the functional indices not only return to the initial level but substantially go above it (Figure 7). This phenomenon received the name of long term delayed training effect (LDTE)" (PDF 535 / p.524).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's framing: the LDTE is the same law as the session overshoot ([[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]]), acting over weeks. Inference: this sentence states the link between the two levels that [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] records as unstated on PDF 530; it is still an assertion, since no mechanism for the long level is given here.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — When placing a concentrated strength or SPP block in the year and explaining to staff why the athlete will be flat during it. The list of sports gives the range the author claims: running, jumping, volleyball, tennis, rowing, judo, weightlifting.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: the page says the studies "convincingly" showed it but describes none of them (no populations, loads or data). Two durations sit a page apart: concentrated SPP stages of "10-12 weeks" here (PDF 535 / p.524) and, in the next list, "the tendency has been for the stages to last anywhere from 4-12 weeks" (PDF 536 / p.525). Keep each number with its locator. The loads in every case are "strength loads" or SPP, including in running and rowing. Inference: this is not evidence of an LDTE after aerobic or distance loading, which Chapter 6 says is documented only after altitude training ([[claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training]]); the two passages describe different loads, so they are not in conflict. Calling the LDTE "supercompensation" also inherits the book's internal dispute over that word ([[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]]).
    23	
    24	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own sport list for the finding, from running and jumping to weightlifting and judo (PDF 535 / p.524). The 9.1 restatement of the LDTE rules and Fig 7 is recorded on [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]; the triple-jump case he gives with them is [[case-study--triple-jumper-annual-cycle-two-strength-blocks-fig-8]].
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]] (6.10), [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]], [[claim--ldte-in-endurance-training-documented-only-after-altitude-training]], [[claim--adaptive-reconstruction-vs-supercompensation]], [[case-study--triple-jumper-annual-cycle-two-strength-blocks-fig-8]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]
