# In Cyclic and Team Sports, Raise Threshold Speed First, Then Glycolytic Capacity; Build Heart Volume Before Contractile Power; Hold the Highest Intensity for the Precompetitive Stage

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's sequence for endurance intensification (9.1 §1.8, PDF 546-547 / pp.535-536, checked against the page images):
1. **Moderate intensity first, for the heart.** "moderate intensity work leads to economic activity of the cardio-vascular, respiratory and other body systems," lowering heart load, which "substantially decreases the certainty of myocardial dystrophy and creates favourable conditions for peripheral circulatory reactions and adequate hemodynamics. Obviously, it is expedient to have an organization of training that oversees beginning with an increase in heart volume and after this, increasing the power of its contractile function, which is achieved from an even greater increase in training load intensity" (PDF 546 / p.535).
2. **High intensity late.** "work with high intensity should not begin before the differentiated regional vessel reactions are firmly stabilized, that is, practically up to the precompetitive stage (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25, 26, 284, 285, 294, 295)" (PDF 546).
3. **Threshold speed before glycolysis.** "Study of the foremost practical trial has convincingly shown that first of all, it is necessary to increase the level of speed on the AT level with extensive quality interval running. This ensures favourable conditions for transition from development of speed on the AT level to development of the glycolytic abilities and buffering capabilities of the body. Creation of a solid base in this manner leads to further effective use of more intense means (Nyrmekivi, Piamat, 91)" (PDF 547 / p.536; the name is spelled "Nurmekiwi" on PDF 544).
4. **Summary for cyclic and team sports.** "work on optimal speed (on the anaerobic threshold level) and its increases, makes it possible to have level increases in the heart cavity volume and after this, myocardial power forming adequate peripheral vessel reactions and consequently the morpho-functional improvement in the slow and fast contracting muscle fibers" (PDF 547).
He also rejects "endurance development through speed, that is, through intense anaerobic work," noting that short distances run faster than competition speed "activate economically and functionally unfavourable mechanisms of energy provision" in middle and long distance runners (Tyurin, Shirkovetz, 115, and others) (PDF 546).

**Why it works** — The page's reasoning is structural: volume of the heart and peripheral vessel reactions must be in place before contractile power and high-intensity work can be used without overload ([[claim--premature-intensification-harms-heart-mitochondria-and-support-motor-system]]).

**When to apply** — In planning the conditioning year for an endurance or team-sport athlete. Eric's baseline: "Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124, Explicit). Inference: the baseline's below-threshold aerobic work fits step 1; Verkhoshansky's step 3 then moves to work at threshold speed before glycolytic work, which the baseline does not address. Eric's baseline: glycolytic conditioning "is still not a primary target in season, but staff do program it in the off-season" (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)).

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: the "foremost practical trial" (Nurmekivi and Piamat) is not described, and the heart-volume-then-power order is stated as "obviously ... expedient," not shown. The page talks about "cyclical and team sports" together but all its examples are distance runners, rowers and the like. Inference: in football, the 4.5 m/s ceiling and alactic priority in the baseline (line 116) set a different frame; carry over the order, not the running prescriptions.

**Example** — Nurmekivi's order as quoted: raise AT-level speed with extensive interval running, then develop "the glycolytic abilities and buffering capabilities of the body" (PDF 547 / p.536).

26	# Burlakova's Rowers: Training at Threshold Heart Rate Plus 20 bpm Built Economy and a Base; Plus 30 bpm Raised Power Faster but Built No Base
27	
28	**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 547-549 / pp.536-538, checked against the page images): "In an eight week experiment, in which four groups of rowers-canoe/kayakers participated (19 in each group), to test the effectiveness of four training regimes for development of aerobic abilities. It included work on pulse rate, corresponding to the anaerobic threshold: AT; AT + 10bpm; AT +20bpm and AT +30bpm (Burlakova, 9). The most effective appeared to be the two latter regimes." AT +20 bpm "served to increase economy of the functional systems and increased their activeness. There was a decrease in the concentration of blood lactate during execution of the standard work, a decrease in maximum heart rate with an increase in work power, and there was a significant shortening of time for heart rate recovery after work." AT +30 bpm "brings about a completely different change. It characterizes first of all, a statistically significant increase in work power (in the other training regimes the increase was not statistically significant) with no change in economy and activeness in the energy provision systems" (PDF 548 / p.537). Conclusion: "the AT + 20bpm regime should be considered the most effective, that is, it creates the necessary base for the following increase in sports results. The second of these regimes (AT +30bpm) even though it gives a sharper (faster) increase in results, it does not create a base for future work and the use of it in the preparation of rowers (especially juniors) should be very limited (Burlakova, 9)" (PDF 549 / p.538).
29	
30	**Why it works** — The page judges the regimes by what they change: +20 bpm changed economy markers (lactate at standard work, recovery heart rate); +30 bpm changed power only. Inference: Verkhoshansky prefers the regime that changes the base because, in his 1.8 argument, power gains without a base "do not last very long" ([[principle--intensify-gradually-toward-the-main-competitions-not-early-fig-12]]).
31	
32	**When to apply** — When setting training heart rates for an aerobic block in rowing or similar sports, and as an example of judging a regime by economy markers as well as by power. Eric's baseline: "Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124, Explicit). Inference: Burlakova's best aerobic regime sat 20 bpm above threshold, not below it. The populations differ (rowers and canoe-kayakers versus football players), and the baseline's threshold is "the age-based method" (line 119, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q20)) while the page does not say how AT was set, so this is a difference to note, not a contest.
33	
34	**When NOT to apply** — `supported`: design, group size, duration and outcomes are described, and the page reports significance for power. But only power is said to be tested for significance; the economy changes for +20 bpm are not given numbers, and "the most effective" is the author's judgment. "a decrease in maximum heart rate with an increase in work power" is ambiguous in translation. The claim that +30 bpm "does not create a base for future work" is not supported by any follow-up period within the eight weeks.
35	
36	**Example** — The four groups of 19 trained for eight weeks at AT, AT +10, AT +20 and AT +30 bpm; only AT +30 gave a statistically significant rise in work power, while AT +20 lowered lactate at standard work and shortened heart-rate recovery (PDF 547-548 / pp.536-537).

Findings: "training, with the use of speed loads and individual AT levels (20-30% of the total volume) gives a real increase in AT and sports results in the 5000m run. If with these volumes they use loads going above the individual AT level by 0.2m/sec, it leads to a decrease in the initial AT level and an insignificant increase in the sports result." And "the greatest effect of threshold loads occurs in those cases when their volume corresponds to the level of preparation of the athlete, in which their volume, expressed as a percent of the total volume of running loads, increases according to the increase in the preparation of the athlete." The recommended threshold volumes, as a share of total distance work, by the runner's AT speed:
48	- 3.6-3.9 m/s: up to 15%.
49	- 4.0-4.3 m/s: 15-20%.
50	- 4.4-4.7 m/s: 20-25%.
51	- 4.8-5.1 m/s: 25-30%.
52	- 5.2-5.5 m/s: 30-35%.
53	- "For runners, on a higher level of preparation this volume can reach 40%."

133	
134	**What it is** — 9.1 §1.9, "The phenomena of decreasing of immunological reactivity" (PDF 552-553 / pp.541-542, checked against the page images). He lists six contributors to "disturbance of immunological homeostasis": "a) increasing imbalance in the humerol-hormonal regulatory function during intense sports loads; b) exhaustion of the sympathoadrenal system and hypophyseal-adrenocortical hystem; c) progressive increases in activeness of the trophotropic mechanisms; d) accompanied increases in tonus of the centrally formed parasympathetic section of the vegetative (autonomic) nervous system; e) increased permeability of the Hematoencephalic barrier for several hormones and; f) deep metabolic changes arising in the middle of the mix (Levando et al., 70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." The numbers: "If illness in athletes before beginning the training year with moderate intensity loads is 1, then in the competitive period tied in with intensified trainings, it increases 5-10 times, and immediately before competition up to 25 times (Levando, 76). It is known that on the day before and during many major competitions, up to 40% of the athletes had an illness that decreased their potential and ability to achieve high results (Levando, 69, Levando et al.70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." And: "at the peak of trainedness in weightlifters, wrestlers and other athletes, there is frequently observed a decrease in resistance to the influence of cold and cold type illness (Meerson, Pshennikova, 78)."

This is tied in with inadequately high intensity of the loads used" (Aronov et al, 2); in children, "an optimal training load in young athletes increases the immunological reactivenss in comparison to children not participating in sport. But, during intense loads, the immune-reactiveness of children decreases (Suharev, Suhanova, 110)" (PDF 552 / p.541).

"Levando, 76" uses the reference number that 9.1 elsewhere gives to Meerson (for example "Meerson, 76," PDF 534). Inference: the citation may be misnumbered. The six mechanisms are listed, not argued. Footnote 17 (unsigned) defines the "Hematoencephalic barrier" as the blood-brain barrier (PDF 552 / p.541).
141	
142	**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: up to 40% of athletes at many major competitions had an illness on the day before or during the event that lowered their performance (PDF 553 / p.542).

152

Even if the body was capable of spontaneously restoring its defense functions when it has expressed exhaustion, it requires a greater amount of time during which the body is vulnerable to unfavorable factors (chilling, change in climate or geographic zone, contact with sick individuals and so on). In separate instances (after serious illness, a break in adaptation) the period of restitution can be dragged out over several months, that provokes repeat illnesses. # Dubinin's 800 m Runners: Early Intensive Preparation Led in Winter and Early Summer, Aerobic-First Preparation Led at the Main Competitions (Fig 13)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 547 / p.536, checked against the page image): Fig 13 gives "the data from experimental annual training programs of two groups of high level middle distance runners (Dubinin, 51). In one group, (A) the task was to develop the aerobic sources of energy and to increase running economy. The main portion of the distance methods of running was taken up by running under the anaerobic threshold level. In group B training, the objective was to improve anaerobic sources of energy ... For this, they used more intense training than in group A. preparation for which began even in the first stage of the preparatory period." Result: "athletes using the intense preparation method (group B) had a higher result in the winter and in the first starts of the summer competitive season. However at the beginning of the main starts later on in the season, the athletes in group A came out on a higher level of sports preparation." The Fig 13 caption (PDF 548 / p.537) adds details the text does not: "Dynamics of the sport results in the 800 m running (above) and the training loads parameters (intensive loads - in black, extensive loads - in grey) in the two groups of the female athletes (the experimental group A and the control group B) during the yearly cycle of preparation."

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky's reading: "intensification of training in the preparatory period does not guarantee achieving high absolute results in the competitive period" (PDF 547). Fig 13, read from the page image (approximate readings): the result axis runs from 2.06 to 1.54 (min.sec), faster upward. Group A's line starts about 2.04 near I, group B's about 2.02; they cross near V at about 2.00; by the right end A is near 1.54 and B near 1.56. Monthly load bars (X to IX, no unit printed, scale 0-300): group B's black intensive share is present from X and runs roughly 40-95 through the year, with totals falling from about 200 in X to about 60 in IX; group A has almost no black until II-IV, then intensive load rises to about 50-80 from VI to IX, while totals stay about 165-290.

**When to apply** — When choosing between an aerobic-first and an intensity-first preparatory period for a sport with a clear main competition. # Burlakova's Rowers: Training at Threshold Heart Rate Plus 20 bpm Built Economy and a Base; Plus 30 bpm Raised Power Faster but Built No Base

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 547-549 / pp.536-538, checked against the page images): "In an eight week experiment, in which four groups of rowers-canoe/kayakers participated (19 in each group), to test the effectiveness of four training regimes for development of aerobic abilities. It included work on pulse rate, corresponding to the anaerobic threshold: AT; AT + 10bpm; AT +20bpm and AT +30bpm (Burlakova, 9). The most effective appeared to be the two latter regimes." AT +20 bpm "served to increase economy of the functional systems and increased their activeness. There was a decrease in the concentration of blood lactate during execution of the standard work, a decrease in maximum heart rate with an increase in work power, and there was a significant shortening of time for heart rate recovery after work." AT +30 bpm "brings about a completely different change. It characterizes first of all, a statistically significant increase in work power (in the other training regimes the increase was not statistically significant) with no change in economy and activeness in the energy provision systems" (PDF 548 / p.537). Conclusion: "the AT + 20bpm regime should be considered the most effective, that is, it creates the necessary base for the following increase in sports results. The second of these regimes (AT +30bpm) even though it gives a sharper (faster) increase in results, it does not create a base for future work and the use of it in the preparation of rowers (especially juniors) should be very limited (Burlakova, 9)" (PDF 549 / p.538).

**Why it works** — The page judges the regimes by what they change: +20 bpm changed economy markers (lactate at standard work, recovery heart rate); +30 bpm changed power only. Inference: Verkhoshansky prefers the regime that changes the base because, in his 1.8 argument, power gains without a base "do not last very long" ([[principle--intensify-gradually-toward-the-main-competitions-not-early-fig-12]]).

**When to apply** — When setting training heart rates for an aerobic block in rowing or similar sports, and as an example of judging a regime by economy markers as well as by power. Eric's baseline: "Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124, Explicit). Inference: Burlakova's best aerobic regime sat 20 bpm above threshold, not below it. The populations differ (rowers and canoe-kayakers versus football players), and the baseline's threshold is "the age-based method" (line 119, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q20)) while the page does not say how AT was set, so this is a difference to note, not a contest.

**When NOT to apply** — `supported`: design, group size, duration and outcomes are described, and the page reports significance for power. But only power is said to be tested for significance; the economy changes for +20 bpm are not given numbers, and "the most effective" is the author's judgment. "a decrease in maximum heart rate with an increase in work power" is ambiguous in translation. The claim that +30 bpm "does not create a base for future work" is not supported by any follow-up period within the eight weeks.

**Example** — The four groups of 19 trained for eight weeks at AT, AT +10, AT +20 and AT +30 bpm; only AT +30 gave a statistically significant rise in work power, while AT +20 lowered lactate at standard work and shortened heart-rate recovery (PDF 547-548 / pp.536-537).

**Related** — [[principle--intensify-gradually-toward-the-main-competitions-not-early-fig-12]], [[heuristic--endurance-intensification-order-threshold-speed-then-glycolytic-heart-volume-then-power]], [[heuristic--zorin-threshold-run-volume-scaled-to-the-runners-at-speed]], [[claim--physiological-thresholds-are-ranges-and-athletes-regulate-performance-by-feel]], [[framework--functional-economy-trained-vs-untrained-and-three-levels-fig-11]]

# Scale Threshold-Pace Volume to the Runner's Own Threshold Speed: From Up to 15% of Distance Work to 35-40%, and Do Not Run Above It (Zorin)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 549 / p.538, checked against the page image) reports an experiment by Zorin (57) whose purpose was "to evaluate the effectiveness of using distance loads on the AT level in the training of long distance runners. Also, to determine the optimal volume of threshold loads taking into consideration the individual levels of preparation of the runners." Findings: "training, with the use of speed loads and individual AT levels (20-30% of the total volume) gives a real increase in AT and sports results in the 5000m run. If with these volumes they use loads going above the individual AT level by 0.2m/sec, it leads to a decrease in the initial AT level and an insignificant increase in the sports result." And "the greatest effect of threshold loads occurs in those cases when their volume corresponds to the level of preparation of the athlete, in which their volume, expressed as a percent of the total volume of running loads, increases according to the increase in the preparation of the athlete." The recommended threshold volumes, as a share of total distance work, by the runner's AT speed:
- 3.6-3.9 m/s: up to 15%.
- 4.0-4.3 m/s: 15-20%.
- 4.4-4.7 m/s: 20-25%.
- 4.8-5.1 m/s: 25-30%.
- 5.2-5.5 m/s: 30-35%.
- "For runners, on a higher level of preparation this volume can reach 40%."

**Why it works** — Inference: the page gives no mechanism; the 0.2 m/s result shows that a small step above threshold turns the load into the anaerobic work the section warns slows aerobic development ("work in the anaerobic zone, as was talked about above, slows down development of aerobic abilities," PDF 549).

**When to apply** — When prescribing threshold work for distance runners or other endurance athletes with a measured threshold speed. Inference: the principle (threshold share rises with the athlete's level, and pace stays at, not above, the individual threshold) can be used even where the running speeds do not fit.

**When NOT to apply** — `supported` for the experiment, whose aim, population and two conditions are described, but no sample size or statistics are given. The five-band table is a recommendation; the page does not show which data it was derived from beyond the 20-30% result. It is for long-distance runners. Inference: in football the baseline's general speed ceiling "around 4.5 m/s" for aerobic work (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 124, Explicit) sits inside the 4.4-4.7 m/s band, but that ceiling is a cap for below-threshold work, not a measured threshold speed, so the table does not transfer.

**Example** — Zorin's finding as reported: 20-30% of total volume at the individual AT raised AT and 5000 m results; running the same volume 0.2 m/s above AT lowered the initial AT level (PDF 549 / p.538).

# Intense Training in 1500 m Runners From October to March: Glycolytic Enzymes and Fast-Fibre Size Up, Oxidative Enzymes, Slow-Fibre Size and VO2 Max Down (Neumann, Table 3)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 549 / p.538, checked against the page image): "work in the anaerobic zone, as was talked about above, slows down development of aerobic abilities. As a result, a significant increase in training intensity, of anaerobic functional abilities increase and the aerobic decrease (Table 3)." Table 3, "Influence of intense training in 1500m runners on the functional base of muscle cells and maximum oxygen utilization (G.Neumann, 1990)," as printed (October, March):
- "Productivity of energy exchange in the fast twitch fibers (%)": 10, 20. Then "Glycolytic": 10, 20; "Oxidative": 15, 3.
- "Cross section of muscle fibers (MKM2)": slow twitch 5888, 5312; fast twitch 5856, 6080.
- "Enzyme activeness in FG fibers (millimoles per sec.Kg)": "Citrate synthase (oxidative)" 700, 430; "Phosphogylcerol kinase (glycolytic)" 2550, 3650.
- "Maximum oxygen utilization, ml/kg per min.": 71.0, 67.0.
His conclusion (PDF 550 / p.539): "in the preparatory period when training is directed mainly to the development of aerobic power, the use of such loads should be limited."

**Why it works** — The table shows the shift the text names: glycolytic markers up, oxidative markers down. Inference: in percentage terms citrate synthase fell by about 39% and phosphoglycerate kinase rose by about 43%, slow-fibre area fell about 10% and fast-fibre area rose about 4%, and VO2 max fell 4.0 ml/kg/min (about 6%).

**When to apply** — As a warning that a preparatory period dominated by intense running can trade oxidative capacity for glycolytic capacity in the muscle itself, not only in performance tests. Inference: it is the muscle-level counterpart of the Dubinin result ([[case-study--dubinin-800m-runners-aerobic-vs-intensive-preparation-fig-13]]).

**When NOT to apply** — `supported`: the population (1500 m runners), the condition (intense training), the two time points and the values are printed; the number of runners, the training content and any statistics are not. The first block is hard to read as printed: a row "Productivity of energy exchange in the fast twitch fibers (%)" carries 10 and 20, the same values as the "Glycolytic" row under it, and the "Oxidative" row falls from 15 to 3; Inference: the first row is probably a heading whose values were repeated in error. "MKM2" is a transliteration of square micrometres. There is no control group, so the season itself, not intensity alone, could account for part of the change.

**Example** — From the table: citrate synthase in fast glycolytic fibres fell from 700 to 430 while VO2 max fell from 71.0 to 67.0 ml/kg per min between October and March (PDF 549 / p.538).

# The Large Training Cycle (Fig 14): Block A Local SPP at Moderate Competition Speed, Block B Intensify the Competition Exercise, Block C Compete

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.8, PDF 550 / p.539, checked against the page image) first names the risk of the gradual route: "if a significant portion of time is devoted to execution of the sports events at a moderate speed, then at the moment of major competition there will simply not be enough time to adapt the body to the speed work regime," and "in cyclical and team type sports ... the muscle groups that carry the main load a will remain behind the vegetative systems according to tempo and level of functional improvement" (Verkhoshansky, 24, 25). His answer: "it is expedient at the beginning of the big training cycle, when the competitive exercises are executed at a moderate speed, to selectively intensify the motor system work regime with special physical (including strength) preparation. The exercises should be directed locally to those muscle groups that are mainly involved in competitive conditions. After this, according to the amount of resolution of this task, it follows to use quality intensification of the competitive exercise by gradually increasing execution almost up to maximum speed." The scheme: "A. Means (loads) ensuring morpho-functional specialization of the body as a whole and primarily the locomotor system in correspondence with the specific competitive activity - task of getting ahead with the body preparation for speed work ... B. Means (loads) directed to the intensification of the motor regime, using primarily the competitive exercise. C. Competition activities (loads) with the increasing of speed." Fig 14 (PDF 551 / p.540, read from the image) has three panels over "Basic stage Block A," "Special stage Block B" and "Competition stage Block C." Top: overlapping load humps A, B, C, with the result curve V falling below its start V0 during A and rising through B and C to V1 (the gain marked ΔV). Middle, "TRAINING RUNNING SPEED": a rising curve that starts at "Optimal speed (threshold level - V_OPT)," passes "Training max speed - V_MAX" around the B-C boundary, and approaches "Competition max speed (top speed - V_TOP)" by the end of C. Bottom, "RUNNING LOADS VOLUME": V_OPT volume peaks early in A and declines; V_MAX volume peaks in B; V_TOP volume peaks in C. The caption calls V "the hypothetical trend of sport result."

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky: the coach still "intensifies the entire work regime of the body in conditions approaching the competitive," but "thanks to the preliminary morpho-functional preparation of the motor and other physiological systems of the body, this does not lead to its overload" (PDF 550). Inference: block A solves the two problems he names, too little time to adapt to speed and the working muscles lagging the cardiorespiratory systems, by raising the local muscular "motor regime" with SPP while running speed stays moderate.

**When to apply** — When building a year (or a long off-season) toward a target competition period: a local, strength-heavy SPP block first, then progressive speed in the competition exercise, then competition. Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming 'compass'" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: Fig 14 orders the same qualities across one cycle, with speed held to the late blocks.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: Fig 14 is a "principle scheme" and the result curve is labelled "hypothetical"; the page refers to other studies for details (Verkhoshansky, 25, 284, 285; Verkhoshansky, Zaleev, 29). The panels are drawn for running (threshold, training max, competition top speed); the page gives no durations for A, B or C. Inference: the dip in V during block A is the LDTE pattern ([[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]]), so a sport with competitions every week cannot use block A in season.

**Example** — The caption's block A: "stage of the concentrated training loads finalised to the morpho-functional specialization of the body as a whole and primarily the locomotor system in correspondence with the specific competitive activity" (PDF 551 / p.540).

# Soviet Sprinters Led East German Sprinters at 13-18 but Stalled After 18, Which Galukhin Blamed on Premature Intensification

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky carries the 1.8 argument to multi-year training (9.1 §1.8, PDF 550-552 / pp.539-541, checked against the page images): "All of what has been said above about the optimal regime of development of the adaptational process in the yearly cycle, relates fully to multiyear training. Premature intensification and preparation of young athletes does not create favourable conditions for progress in their future mastery." His example: "in the preparation of sprinters, Soviet coaches for many years were oriented not to creating a solid foundation for achieving high level results, but to fast tempo increases in achievement based on narrow specialized means. This led to early mobilization of reserves possessed by young athletes which exhausted their capabilities and as a result, at 18-20 years of age, to stabilization of results in comparison to stronger foreign athletes (Galukhin, 41, Kniazeva, 63)." The comparison: "at age 13-18 the mean results of the strongest runners in the USSR surpassed those of East German runners and after 18 years of age results of soviet sprinters stabilized and increased insignificantly up to 20-23 years of age when at the same time the East German runners were found to have improved concluding with world class results in the 100 and 200 meters" (PDF 551 / p.540). The cause, "as shown by analysis of the training methods, was in the incorrect distribution of means and methods of training in the process of multiyear planning, which is in the premature intensification of training (Galukhin, 41)." Children's youth sports schools "most frequently used means and methods characteristic of high level sprinters with sufficiently high volumes" (PDF 552 / p.541).

**Why it works** — The counter-finding (Kniazeva, 63; PDF 552 / p.541): "on the beginning stage of sports specialization, improvement in the functional and physical preparation is the base for future mastery. With less intense but more varied exercises, not only was there no decrease in the level of increase in sports results, but it created better conditions for further sports improvement of young runners specializing in the short distances."

**When to apply** — When a young athlete's programme copies an elite one. Eric's baseline: "Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 173, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the page gives a performance reason for the same stance, aimed at the years before college.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: no numbers, sample sizes or training data are given for either country, and the cause is the analysts' attribution. Inference: other differences between the two systems (selection, coaching, and East German doping programmes of that era, which the page does not mention) could explain part of the gap, so the comparison cannot isolate training intensity. Kniazeva's result is stated without design details.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: Soviet sprinters led at 13-18 and "stabilized and increased insignificantly up to 20-23 years of age," while East German sprinters went on to world-class 100 and 200 m results (PDF 551 / p.540).

# Intense Loads and the Peak of Form Depress Immunity: Illness Rises 5-10 Times in the Competitive Period and up to 25 Times Just Before Competition

**What it is** — 9.1 §1.9, "The phenomena of decreasing of immunological reactivity" (PDF 552-553 / pp.541-542, checked against the page images). Verkhoshansky: "It has long been known that extreme physical and psycho-emotional loads in contemporary sport have a depressing influence on the defense systems of the body (Kassil et al, 61, Surkina et al. 109)." He lists six contributors to "disturbance of immunological homeostasis": "a) increasing imbalance in the humerol-hormonal regulatory function during intense sports loads; b) exhaustion of the sympathoadrenal system and hypophyseal-adrenocortical hystem; c) progressive increases in activeness of the trophotropic mechanisms; d) accompanied increases in tonus of the centrally formed parasympathetic section of the vegetative (autonomic) nervous system; e) increased permeability of the Hematoencephalic barrier for several hormones and; f) deep metabolic changes arising in the middle of the mix (Levando et al., 70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." The numbers: "If illness in athletes before beginning the training year with moderate intensity loads is 1, then in the competitive period tied in with intensified trainings, it increases 5-10 times, and immediately before competition up to 25 times (Levando, 76). It is known that on the day before and during many major competitions, up to 40% of the athletes had an illness that decreased their potential and ability to achieve high results (Levando, 69, Levando et al.70, Suzdalnitzky et al. 108)." And: "at the peak of trainedness in weightlifters, wrestlers and other athletes, there is frequently observed a decrease in resistance to the influence of cold and cold type illness (Meerson, Pshennikova, 78)."

**Why it works** — Verkhoshansky ties it to intensity, not training as such: in rowers, loads "lead to a decrease in immune reactiveness, and its recovery takes place very slowly. This is tied in with inadequately high intensity of the loads used" (Aronov et al, 2); in children, "an optimal training load in young athletes increases the immunological reactivenss in comparison to children not participating in sport. But, during intense loads, the immune-reactiveness of children decreases (Suharev, Suhanova, 110)" (PDF 552 / p.541).

**When to apply** — When planning the weeks before a main competition and the competitive period: the page puts the highest illness rate exactly where performance matters most. Inference: hygiene and exposure control matter most in the precompetitive week, and a cluster of colds then is a load signal as well as a medical one ([[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: all figures are cited (Levando and others) with no populations, definitions of "illness," or study design. "Levando, 76" uses the reference number that 9.1 elsewhere gives to Meerson (for example "Meerson, 76," PDF 534). Inference: the citation may be misnumbered. The six mechanisms are listed, not argued. Footnote 17 (unsigned) defines the "Hematoencephalic barrier" as the blood-brain barrier (PDF 552 / p.541).

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own: up to 40% of athletes at many major competitions had an illness on the day before or during the event that lowered their performance (PDF 553 / p.542).

**Related** — [[heuristic--colds-under-prolonged-loading-signal-cut-load-and-add-general-restoration]], [[heuristic--immune-restoration-is-the-slowest-so-protect-athletes-after-peaks-and-illness]], [[framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring]], [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[principle--intensify-gradually-toward-the-main-competitions-not-early-fig-12]]

chapter: "9.1"
topic: slow immune restoration
category: [immunity, recovery, illness, return-to-training]
confidence: untested

# The Immune System Restores More Slowly Than Other Systems, So the Vulnerable Window Outlasts the Feeling of Recovery; After Serious Illness It Can Take Months

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky (9.1 §1.9, PDF 553 / p.542, checked against the page image): "The restorative processes in the immune system are, to a significant degree, slower in comparison with other physiological systems. Even if the body was capable of spontaneously restoring its defense functions when it has expressed exhaustion, it requires a greater amount of time during which the body is vulnerable to unfavorable factors (chilling, change in climate or geographic zone, contact with sick individuals and so on). In separate instances (after serious illness, a break in adaptation) the period of restitution can be dragged out over several months, that provokes repeat illnesses. In similar situations athletes practically have to stop training and frequently stop participating in sport (Surkina et al. 109)." The rowing finding on the previous page agrees: immune reactiveness falls and "its recovery takes place very slowly" (Aronov et al, 2; PDF 552 / p.541).

**Why it works** — The page states the time difference but no mechanism. Inference: if performance markers recover faster than immune function, an athlete can look ready while still exposed, which is the risk the page names (chilling, travel, contact with sick people).

**When to apply** — After a peak, a hard competitive block or a serious illness: plan travel, cold exposure and contact with sick people as risks for longer than performance recovery suggests. Inference: in football, the post-season travel and the return after a significant illness are the obvious windows; the page gives no durations for the ordinary case.

**When NOT to apply** — Rated `untested`: no study or data is described; "several months" refers only to "separate instances (after serious illness, a break in adaptation)." The page gives no way to measure immune recovery. Return to training after illness is a medical decision; this passage does not set criteria.

**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own list of the risks during the slow window: "chilling, change in climate or geographic zone, contact with sick individuals" (PDF 553 / p.542).

This adds a within-book contradiction to the contest recorded above. See [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] and [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]].
5	+**Also in 9.1** — Verkhoshansky's own paper uses supercompensation without the 1.16 reservation (both checked against the page images). One of the three bases of the constructive effect is "supercompensation of the ingredients, that are used up during the time of work (substrates serving as sources of energy and different structural and enzymatic proteins)" (9.1 §1.5, PDF 530 / p.519), and by the "rule of V.Engelgard," "in normal functioning biosystems the restorative process is always potentially greater and supersedes the processes of breakdown (the phenomena of supercompensation)" (PDF 533 / p.522). This adds a within-book contradiction to the contest recorded above. See [[framework--two-levels-of-the-constructive-effect-of-adaptation]] and [[claim--single-stress-depresses-then-raises-protein-synthesis-above-baseline-fig-5]]. The next paragraphs go further (PDF 534 / p.523, checked against the page image): "The law of supercompensation also applies to creatine phosphate, the enzymatic and structural proteins, to the phosolipids, and to a number of mitochondria in the muscle fibers - in a word, for all products and structures, which to one or another degree, were expended or destroyed during the muscular activity and are resynthesized during the time of rest (Yakovlev, 144)," and Fig 9 has a box "Super compensation of CP and glycogen contents" (PDF 538 / p.527). Both state the opposite of the 1.16 sentence on other biochemicals. See [[claim--yakovlev-glycogen-supercompensation-wave-fig-6]] and [[framework--yakovlev-work-and-recovery-biosynthesis-chain-fig-9]].

27:**When NOT to apply** — **Contested inside the book.** Verkhoshansky's Addendum paper (9.1, "Dr. Yuri Verkhoshansky, Translated from the Russian by Dr. Michael Yessis"; PDF p. 515 / printed p. 504, checked against the page image) restates the emergence-period rule the other way round: "In the period of LDTE realization, volume concentrated loads are handled by the body relatively easily and without harm to the body, but intense loads negatively react to the work volume" (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image). Its own example then agrees with Chapter 6: an "insignificant increase" in specialised strength volume "(by only a few percent)" to "maintain" the achieved level "led to a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results" (same page, checked against the page image). Inference: the Addendum sentence may be a translation slip: its own example fits Chapter 6, and the Addendum is a separate translation of Verkhoshansky's text, which makes a translation slip plausible. The book prints both. The authors give no number for "small volume" or for how long technical emphasis should wait. Inference: for skills that need daily practice (team-sport play), technique cannot simply wait for the strength block to end; the rule is written for "high level athletes" in events where the competitive action can be isolated, and they mention the conjugate system "successively introduces different modes of loading ... rather than separating them in time" (PDF p. 376),
29:**Example** — Verkhoshansky's own, from the Addendum (PDF p. 536 / printed p. 525, checked against the page image): the text says its Figure 8 shows that "in triple jumpers," concentrated specialised strength loads in March-April were followed by a rise in speed-strength and results in May-June; raising strength volume "by only a few percent" to hold the gain then brought "a fast decrease in speed-strength and sports results." The page switches from plural to singular here: the volume rise was "as believed by the athlete," and "the athlete lost his chance to be selected in the qualifying competitions for a place on the national team." Inference: an off-season strength block ending in March would hand over to technical and speed emphasis in April with strength volume held, not raised.
31:**Related** — [[principle--long-term-delayed-training-effect-from-volume-above-the-optimum]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[claim--excess-heavy-strength-volume-impairs-speed-strength-and-technique]], [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--keep-event-specific-competitive-stress-in-preparation]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--realization-mesocycle-taper-prescription]], [[principle--technical-mastery-needs-competition-intensity-practice]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]] (6.12.2, the same strength-then-technique question from a later passage); [[heuristic--loading-reduction-for-the-delayed-effect-must-outlast-1-2-weeks]] (6.12.2, the reduced-loading stage after large volumes must last far longer than the usual 1-2 week unload; its "no more volume" instruction is rule 2 here); From 9.1: [[case-study--triple-jumper-annual-cycle-two-strength-blocks-fig-8]] (Fig 8 read from the image: two strength blocks, X-XI and III-IV, and a July barbell rise from about 4 to 16 t)
----
26:**Related** — [[claim--overtraining-is-accumulated-stress-adaptation-imbalance-exhaustion-is-short-term]], [[framework--functions-affected-by-stress-table-8-4-and-motor-control-monitoring]], [[overtraining-and-sleep--samuels/claim--a-sleep-history-belongs-in-overtraining-screening]], [[claim--intense-loads-and-peak-form-depress-immunity-and-raise-illness]] (9.1), [[heuristic--immune-restoration-is-the-slowest-so-protect-athletes-after-peaks-and-illness]] (9.1)
28:**Also in 9.1** — Not checked in this Chapter 8 review. The Chapter 9 material it points to (PDF 552-553) is outside the Chapter 8 source. Verify at the Chapter 9 gate before citing.

== 97
- Issurin's residual training effects (speed fades fastest, 5 ± 3 days; Block Periodization PDF p. 35, as cited in `docs/synthesis/peaking-and-taper-in-season-football.md`) drive speed programming. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q16): "I believe Issurin. It drives our speed programming in the off-season and what drives sprinting recommendations in season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q16)** See
== 101
- The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill, each level a required foundation for the next) is repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)**; was Inferred (transcript + shared course material) [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10; week1-lecture.md pp.23,26]
== 116
- For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39]; claimed again in the inter
== 117
- Glycolytic conditioning is still not a primary target in season, but staff do program it in the off-season. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q19): "It does hold up, but our staff does program it in the off-season." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)**
== 119
- The anaerobic-threshold heart rate in use is the age-based method (the slide deck's max HR = 220-age for men, 226-age for women, threshold at about 85% of that [class-4-2026.md p.27]). Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q20): "Age-based." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q20)** Resolves Tension 6.
== 123
- For speed-power athletes, the aerobic system's main value is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP between bouts), not distance capacity — a better-developed aerobic system means more available energy on play 10, 11, or 12 of a drive, not longer continuous running ability. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md p.9]
== 124
- Aerobic-system training is kept below anaerobic threshold with roughly a 1:1 to 1:2 work:rest ratio and a general speed ceiling around 4.5 m/s, specifically to avoid spilling over into glycolytic-system stress. **Explicit** [week3-lecture.md p.51; 2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.11-12]
== 142
- Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver, not just a training-quality issue. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.27]
== 153
- Recovery is managed through training-load design alone; nothing objective is tracked, sleep included. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q23): "It's handled through training-load design alone. We're not tracking anything objective." **Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q23)**
== 171
- New movement patterns are expected to take roughly 3-4 weeks of practice to become efficient and low-energy-cost, which informs how much proficiency to expect when a new exercise or drill is introduced. **Inferred (transcript)** [2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md pp.6-7]
== 173
- Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
== 185
- In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window. Eric (interview 2026-09-28, Q14): "in football you want to peak every Saturday, but definitely throughout the month of November as you get closer to the postseason ... That's when players need to be at or near their peak as they head into the postseason and playoffs." **Explicit (interview 2

# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months

**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
1984). The authors state training prescription must account for the different
adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
slowest; they recommend gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods

# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months

**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
1984). The authors state training prescription must account for the different
adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
slowest; they recommend gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods

14:# Volume Drives Long-Term Adaptation and Prepares Connective Tissue; Intensify Only After Extensive Low-Intensity Work
16:**What it is** — The authors give volume two roles. First: "The function of the volume of the load consists chiefly of the systematic and prolonged disturbance of the body's homeostasis, which stimulates the mobilisation of its energy resources and plastic reserves. This is the fundamental condition for switching from the acute (specific) reaction ... to the general (non-specific) adaptive reaction, and then to the development of long-term adaptation of the body. Therefore, in each successive annual cycle athletes should execute larger volumes of loading (within optimal limits) to raise and maintain the special work-capacity" (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358, checked against the page image). 
18:Volume alone is not enough: "the influence of the volume can be determined correctly only if one also takes into consideration the magnitude of the loading, its duration and intensity" (PDF p. 369). Magnitude is set "first of all, on the basis of the athlete's qualification": the higher the qualification, the larger the yearly and stage volume, and the share of "specialised loading" grows (Panov 1975; Zhikharevich 1976; Vankov 1977; Matveyev 1977; Gilyazova 1978). The annual volume is "established individually" from the preceding stages; "A more serious task" is the optimal volume per month, stage or phase (same page). On intensity: it "determines the strength and specificity of its effec
22:**When to apply** — Building a multi-year plan (raise annual volume, within limits, as qualification rises) and opening each year with extensive moderate-intensity work before intensifying, especially in jumping and other high-impact events. Eric's baseline: "Progressions in exercise selection, volume, and intensity are kept smooth and gradual by design; abrupt, large changes are treated as a direct injury-risk driver" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 142, Inferred (transcript)). Eric's baseline: "The Vermeil hierarchy of athletic development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill ...)" (line 101, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the author
26:**Example** — The authors' own: gymnastics, weightlifting, high jumping and triple jumping, where joint injury "occurs frequently" if connective tissue has not been prepared by extensive moderate-intensity work before peak dynamic loads (PDF p. 369 / printed p. 358). Inference: a jumper's year would open with weeks of moderate-volume, lower-impact jumping and strength work before depth jumps.
